Course description

Vibrations and waves are everywhere. If you take any system and disturb it from a stable equilibrium, the resultant motion will be waves and vibrations. Think of a guitar string—pluck the string, and it vibrates. The sound waves generated make their way to our ears, and we hear the string’s sound. Our eyes see what’s happening because they receive the electromagnetic waves of the light reflected from the guitar string, so that we can recognize the beautiful sinusoidal waves on the string. In fact, without vibrations and waves, we could not recognize the universe around us at all!

The amazing thing is that we can describe many fascinating phenomena arising from very different physical systems with mathematics. This course will provide you with the concepts and mathematical tools necessary to understand and explain a broad range of vibrations and waves. You will learn that waves come from many interconnected (coupled) objects when they are vibrating together. We will discuss many of these phenomena, along with related topics, including mechanical vibrations and waves, sound waves, electromagnetic waves, optics, and gravitational waves.

Problem 3.1 (16 pts)

The electric field for a TE mode in an infinitely long (in the x direction) perfectly conducting rectangular waveguide (a < b) is given by

    E⃗(x,y,z,t) = E₀ cos(k_y y + φ_y) cos(k_x x − ωt) ẑ

[Figure 1: A perfectly conducting waveguide — a rectangular box drawn in perspective with its long axis along x, extending indefinitely to the right (the open end is drawn with dotted lines and a wavy field pattern inside). The y-axis points up and the z-axis points toward the viewer, both from the origin at the near-left corner. The height of the box along y is labelled a, and the depth along z is labelled b, with a < b. The guide is infinitely long in the x direction.]

(a) Find k_y and φ_y that satisfy the boundary conditions.
(b) Write down the dispersion relation for this mode of the waveguide.
(c) What is the lowest frequency that will propagate in this mode?
(d) What is the magnetic field B⃗(x,y,z,t) associated with the electric field of this mode?


Problem 3.2 (16 pts)

The figure below shows a system of masses. The mass of 2m is connected to an immobile wall with a spring of constant 2k, while the mass of m is connected to an immobile wall with a spring of constant k. The masses are then coupled to each other with an elastic band of length L, under tension T = 2kL. The masses are constrained to move in the x direction only. At equilibrium the masses have the same x position and the springs are uncompressed. There is no friction or gravity. The displacements from equilibrium are small enough (x₁, x₂ ≪ L), so that the tension in the band stays constant.

[Figure 2: A system of coupled oscillators — two vertical walls, one on the left and one on the right, with the region between them drawn in a vertical plane. Axes at the upper left show y pointing up and x pointing right. Near the top of the gap sits a circular mass labelled m, connected by a coil spring of constant k running horizontally to the right-hand wall. Near the bottom sits a circular mass labelled 2m, connected by a coil spring of constant 2k running horizontally to the left-hand wall. The two masses are joined to each other by a vertical elastic band of length L under tension T = 2kL, drawn as a double-headed vertical arrow between them. Each mass carries a small horizontal arrow marking its displacement coordinate: x₂ for the upper mass m, x₁ for the lower mass 2m. Both masses move only in the x direction, so the coupling band tilts slightly when they are displaced.]

(a) Write down the coupled differential equations describing the displacement of the masses from equilibrium {x₁, x₂}.
(b) Find the normal mode frequencies of the system.
(c) On the two figures included on the next page sketch the normal modes of the system; be sure to clearly indicate both the magnitude and direction of the motion of the masses.


Problem 3.3 (16 pts)

(a) An optical fiber consists of a solid rod of material with index of refraction n_f surrounded by a cylindrical shell of material with index n_c. Find the largest angle θ so that a wave incident on the solid rod from air with index n_a remains in the solid rod (express your answer in terms of n_f, n_c, and n_a).

[Figure 3: An optical fiber — a horizontal three-layer slab drawn in cross section. The middle layer, the core, is labelled n_f. Above and below it are cladding layers, both labelled n_c. To the left of the fiber is air, labelled n_a. A ray arrives from the upper left and strikes the flat left end face of the core, making an angle θ with the horizontal fiber axis; θ is marked between the incoming ray and the axis at the entrance face.]

(b) Unpolarized light propagating in vacuum reflects off the surface of a liquid with index n. The reflected ray strikes a screen 25 cm away at a height of 20 cm and is observed to be 100% polarized. What is n?

(c) Consider a medium in which waves propagate with a dispersion relation

    ω² = ω₀² + A²k²

where ω is the wave (angular) frequency, k is the wave number, and ω₀ and A are real constants.

    (i) What is the range of frequencies ω for which waves can propagate?
    (ii) Compute v_phase and v_group. Make a carefully labeled sketch of each as a function of ω in the plots provided.

[Figure 4: Plot the phase/group velocity — two empty grid plots side by side, provided for the student's sketches. The left plot has vertical axis labelled V_p (phase velocity) and horizontal axis labelled ω; the right plot has vertical axis labelled V_g (group velocity) and horizontal axis labelled ω. Both are blank graph paper with no data drawn and no numerical scale.]


Problem 3.4 (16 pts)

A monochromatic beam is incident on N slits, which results in an intensity pattern as a function of angle on a screen some distance away as shown in the figure below. Each slit has a width D and the distance between the centers of the slits is d. The distance between the screen and the slits is very large.

[Figure 5: Interference pattern due to N slits — a plot of Intensity (vertical axis, no numerical scale) against sin θ (horizontal axis, no numerical scale). The pattern is symmetric about the center. A tall central principal maximum sits at the middle, flanked by principal maxima of decreasing height on each side: the first-order pair is somewhat shorter than the central one, the second-order pair shorter still, and a small third-order pair is visible farther out. The fourth-order principal maximum is absent — the pattern is flat where it would fall, because the first diffraction minimum suppresses it — and small low bumps resume beyond that point. Between each pair of adjacent principal maxima there are three small subsidiary bumps.]

From the pattern deduce the following:

(a) The number of slits N on which the beam is incident. Explain your reasoning.
(b) The ratio d/D. Explain your reasoning.
(c) Now suppose that the width of the slits is reduced to ~0, while the intensity of the monochromatic beam is increased so that the intensity of the central maximum is unchanged. On top of the plot (showing the original intensity pattern in dashed lines) provided, draw the resulting intensity pattern.

[Figure 6: Plot the resulting intensity pattern as D → 0 — an empty plot frame provided for the student's answer, with the original intensity pattern of Figure 5 reproduced in dashed lines underneath.]


Problem 3.5 (20 pts)

A string of length 2L with mass density µ is placed under tension T and is fixed at both ends. At time t = 0, the displacement of the string is zero everywhere but it is struck so that a transverse velocity is imparted to a section of the string. The initial conditions of the string are (a ≪ L):

    y(x, t = 0) = 0

    ẏ(x, t = 0) = v₀      for L − a ≤ x < L
                = −v₀     for L ≤ x < L + a
                = 0       elsewhere

[Figure 7: The initial transverse velocity of the string at time t = 0; the initial displacement is zero everywhere — a horizontal string stretched between two hatched walls, the left wall at x = 0 and the right wall at x = 2L, with the midpoint x = L marked; the distance from each wall to the midpoint is labelled L. The velocity profile is drawn as a pair of adjacent rectangular pulses straddling the midpoint. Just to the left of x = L a rectangle of width a rises above the string to a height labelled v₀. Immediately to the right of x = L a rectangle of the same width a drops below the string to a depth labelled v₀ (i.e. −v₀). The velocity is zero everywhere else along the string.]

(a) Using the plot (Figure 8) provided, sketch the first three normal modes of vibration for this string, regardless of whether or not they are excited.

[Figure 8: Plot the first three normal modes — three identical empty plots stacked vertically, labelled (1), (2), and (3). Each shows a straight horizontal string at rest spanning the gap between a left and a right hatched wall, provided for the student to draw the mode shapes on.]

(b) What is the amplitude of the n-th normal mode after the string is struck? What is the lowest unexcited mode?

(c) Sketch the displacement of the string at time t = (L/2)√(µ/T) in the plot provided.

[Figure 9: Plot the displacement of the string — a single empty plot showing the straight horizontal string at rest between the left and right hatched walls, provided for the student's sketch.]


Problem 3.6 (18 pts)

A charged particle of mass M and charge +Q is attached to the end of a spring of spring constant k. The spring lies along the x-axis and the equilibrium point is at the origin. The particle is displaced from equilibrium by a distance A in the x direction, and released at t = 0. Assume that the size of the particle is much smaller than A, so it can be treated as a point charge, and that the damping rate is very small.

[Figure 10: An oscillating charge — a vertical wall on the left with a horizontal coil spring of constant k attached to it, extending to the right. At the free end of the spring is a circular particle labelled Q,M. Axes are drawn above the spring: z points up and x points to the right, with the origin at the particle's equilibrium position. The particle oscillates along the x-axis.]

(a) Calculate the electric field radiated by the particle along an arbitrary direction in the x−z plane, at a distance R, where R ≫ A.
(b) Calculate the total time averaged power radiated by the particle.
(c) Assuming that the power radiated does not change appreciably as a function of time, give a simple rough estimate of the time it will take for the particle to decrease its amplitude of oscillation to 1/e of its initial value. Is this assumption realistic?
(d) A more refined estimate can be obtained using that dA/dt = (dA/dE) × (dE/dt), and using the average power radiated over a given cycle for dE/dt. Use this to calculate the time it will take the particle to decrease its oscillation amplitude to 1/e of its initial value.
